questions.skill: Strengthen: evidence that supports the conclusion
questions.stem:
Coach Dani says: 'Our team should train on Saturday mornings instead of Thursday afternoons. More players will come to training.'
Which statement, if true, most strengthens the coach's argument?

options.A: Saturday is the most popular day for sport in Australia.
options.B: The team won more games last year when it trained twice a week.
options.C: Last term, five players often missed Thursday training because of music lessons, and none of the players has anything on Saturday mornings.
options.D: A cricket club uses the park on Saturday afternoons.

questions.explanation: The argument is that more players will turn up on Saturday mornings. The first statement gives direct evidence: players miss Thursdays for a reason that won't apply on Saturday mornings.

distractors.A: about Australia in general, not about these players' attendance
distractors.B: about how often to train, not when
distractors.D: about the afternoon, and says nothing about attendance

questions.skill: Find the assumption the argument needs
questions.stem:
The bakery sold out of sourdough bread every day this week. So next week it should bake more sourdough loaves, because it will sell more of them.
Which assumption does this argument rely on?

options.A: Some customers wanted sourdough but couldn't buy it because it had sold out.
options.B: Sourdough is the bakery's most expensive bread.
options.C: Customers like sourdough more than white bread.
options.D: The bakery sold out of other breads too.

questions.explanation: Selling out only shows that every loaf was bought. To sell MORE, there must have been people who wanted sourdough and missed out. If nobody missed out, baking more would just leave loaves unsold.

distractors.B: price is not needed for the argument
distractors.C: comparing breads is not needed: it only matters whether more sourdough would sell
distractors.D: other breads don't matter to this argument

questions.stem:
Ms Lee says: 'Students who read every night get better spelling marks. So the school should give every student a reading log to fill in each night, and spelling marks will go up.'
Which statement, if true, most weakens Ms Lee's argument?

options.A: Spelling marks at the school were higher this year than last year.
options.B: When a nearby school introduced reading logs, students filled them in but did not read any more than before.
options.C: Some students prefer to read in the morning rather than at night.
options.D: Reading logs cost very little to print.

questions.explanation: Ms Lee assumes the logs will make students read more. Evidence that logs don't change how much students read cuts the link between the logs and better spelling.

distractors.A: says nothing about whether logs would help
distractors.C: a small detail; reading in the morning could still help spelling
distractors.D: this makes the plan easier, so if anything it helps the argument

questions.skill: Strengthen: link the cause to the result
questions.stem:
A councillor says: 'We should put a pedestrian crossing outside the library. It will make the road safer.'
Which statement, if true, best supports the councillor?

options.A: The library is open seven days a week.
options.B: Drivers often speed on other roads in the town.
options.C: Most accidents on that road in the past five years involved people crossing near the library.
options.D: A crossing costs less than a new footpath.

questions.explanation: If most accidents happen to people crossing at that exact spot, a crossing there targets the real danger, so the road would be safer.

distractors.A: shows people visit, but not that crossing there is dangerous
distractors.B: about other roads
distractors.D: about cost, not safety

questions.stem:
Jas says: 'Our class sold more raffle tickets than any other class, so our class must have the best sellers in the school.'
Which statement, if true, most weakens Jas's argument?

options.A: The raffle raised more money than last year's raffle.
options.B: Some classes started selling tickets a day late.
options.C: Jas's class has twice as many students as any other class.
options.D: Jas sold more tickets than anyone else in her class.

questions.explanation: With twice as many students, the class could sell the most tickets even if each student sold fewer than students in other classes. Being 'the best sellers' is about each person, not the total.

distractors.A: about this year versus last year, not about the classes
distractors.B: it weakens a little, but one day is a small difference compared with a class twice the size
distractors.D: about one student, not the class compared with others

questions.stem:
Mr Ito's class voted for a class pet from five choices: lizard, rabbit, guinea pig, fish and cat. No two pets got the same number of votes.
• The guinea pig got more votes than the fish but fewer than the rabbit.
• The lizard got more votes than the rabbit.
Which statement cannot be true?

options.A: The cat got the most votes.
options.C: The fish got more votes than the lizard.
options.D: The cat got fewer votes than the fish.

questions.explanation: From most to fewest votes, the order must have lizard, then rabbit, then guinea pig, then fish (the cat can go anywhere). So the fish can never beat the lizard. The others are possible, e.g. cat first; or cat last (behind the fish); the guinea pig third if the cat is above it.

distractors.A: possible: cat, lizard, rabbit, guinea pig, fish
distractors.B: possible: lizard, rabbit, guinea pig… with the cat below
distractors.D: possible: the cat could come last

questions.stem:
In a secret code, CAT is written as DCW.
Using the same code, how is BIRD written?
questions.explanation: C → D is 1 letter on, A → C is 2 letters on, T → W is 3 letters on. Each letter moves forward by its position in the word. BIRD: B+1 = C, I+2 = K, R+3 = U, D+4 = H, so CKUH.

distractors.A: moved every letter forward 1
distractors.B: moved every letter forward 3
distractors.C: started counting from 0 instead of 1

questions.skill: Spot the mistake in the reasoning
questions.stem:
Every student in the chess club is good at maths. Ruby is good at maths. So Ruby must be in the chess club.
Which statement shows the mistake in this reasoning?

options.A: Not every student in the chess club enjoys maths.
options.B: Ruby might not like playing chess.
options.C: It does not say how many students are in the chess club.
options.D: Students who are not in the chess club can also be good at maths.

questions.explanation: 'All chess club students are good at maths' does not mean 'all students good at maths are in the chess club'. Ruby could be good at maths without being in the club.

distractors.A: enjoying maths isn't part of the argument
distractors.B: true, but it doesn't explain where the logic goes wrong
distractors.C: the number of members doesn't matter here

questions.skill: Spot the mistake: two things happening together
questions.stem:
Ice-cream sales and the number of people with sunburn both go up in summer. So eating ice cream must make people more likely to get sunburnt.
Which statement best explains the mistake?

options.A: Some people eat ice cream in winter.
options.B: Not everyone who gets sunburnt has eaten ice cream.
options.C: Both could be caused by something else: hot, sunny weather.

questions.explanation: Two things rising together doesn't mean one causes the other. Hot, sunny days make people buy ice cream AND spend time in the sun.

distractors.A: doesn't explain why the two go up together
distractors.B: a fair point, but it doesn't show the real reason both rise
distractors.D: true, but not about the mistake in the reasoning

questions.stem:
In a music class, everyone who plays the violin also plays the piano. Nobody who plays the piano plays the drums.
Which statement must be true?

options.A: Everyone who plays the piano plays the violin.
options.B: At least one student plays the drums.
options.C: Every student plays either the piano or the drums.
options.D: Nobody who plays the violin plays the drums.

questions.explanation: Violin players all play piano, and piano players never play drums, so violin players never play drums.

distractors.A: the rule only goes one way: violinists play piano
distractors.B: nothing says anyone plays drums
distractors.C: some students might play neither

questions.stem:
To be entered in the science fair, a project must be finished by Friday and must include a poster. Only projects that win a ribbon are displayed in the library.
Ana: 'My project was finished on Thursday, so it can be entered in the fair.'
Ben: 'Liam's project is displayed in the library, so it must include a poster.'
If the information is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: Ben: a project in the library won a ribbon, so it was entered, so it had a poster ✓. Ana: finishing on time is only one of the two conditions; we don't know if her project has a poster ✗.

distractors.A: Ana forgets the poster rule
distractors.C: Ana's project might not have a poster
distractors.D: Ben's chain of reasoning is sound

questions.skill: Find the assumption the argument needs
questions.stem:
Jai says: 'Our new puppy chewed my school shoes. We need to buy him more chew toys so he leaves our shoes alone.'
Which assumption has Jai made?

options.A: The puppy is less than one year old.
options.B: Having more chew toys will stop the puppy chewing shoes.
options.C: Chew toys are cheaper than school shoes.
options.D: The puppy only chews things that belong to Jai.

questions.explanation: Jai's plan only works if more toys change what the puppy chews. He hasn't shown this: the puppy might chew shoes anyway.

distractors.A: the puppy's age is not part of the argument
distractors.C: a sensible point, but the argument doesn't depend on cost
distractors.D: the argument isn't about whose things get chewed

questions.skill: Best explanation for a surprising fact
questions.stem:
Fewer people visited Lakeside Pool this summer than last summer, even though the weather was just as hot.
Which statement, if true, best explains this?

options.A: A free water park opened nearby at the start of this summer.
options.B: Entry to Lakeside Pool cost the same as last summer.
options.C: Last summer was one of the hottest on record.
options.D: Lakeside Pool opened a new café this summer.

questions.explanation: A free attraction nearby gives people another place to cool off, which explains why fewer came to the pool even in hot weather.

distractors.B: nothing changed, so it can't explain a change
distractors.C: we're told the weather was just as hot this summer
distractors.D: that would attract more people, not fewer

I am thinking of a two-digit number.
• Its digits add up to 11.
• It is odd.
• If you swap its digits, the new number is 27 more than my number.
What is my number?
questions.explanation: Odd numbers whose digits add to 11: 29, 47, 65, 83. Swapping must make the number bigger by 27: 29 → 92 (63 more), 47 → 74 (27 more) ✓, 65 → 56 (smaller), 83 → 38 (smaller). The number is 47.

distractors.B: check the swap clue
distractors.C: check the swap clue
distractors.D: check the swap clue

Lia: 'I got free garlic bread with my pizza, so it must be Tuesday.'
Mo: 'It's Tuesday and I've bought a pizza, so I'll get a free drink and free garlic bread.'

distractors.A: the information doesn't say garlic bread is ONLY on Tuesdays
distractors.B: Lia's conclusion doesn't have to be true

questions.stem:
Mum is 4 times as old as Zoe. In 6 years' time, Mum will be 3 times as old as Zoe.
How old will Zoe be in 6 years' time?

distractors.B: that is Zoe's age now
distractors.C: that is Mum's age in 6 years

Who came second?

questions.stem:
A cinema sold 150 tickets for one show. Adult tickets cost $15 and child tickets cost $9. The tickets sold for $1830 altogether.
How many adult tickets were sold?
questions.explanation: If all 150 were child tickets, they would make 150 × $9 = $1350. The extra $1830 − $1350 = $480 comes from adults, who each pay $6 more: $480 ÷ $6 = 80 adult tickets (and 70 child tickets).

distractors.B: arithmetic slip
distractors.D: divided $1830 by $15

questions.stem: Gear A turns once clockwise. Which way does gear D turn, and how many times?
questions.explanation: Touching gears turn in opposite directions: A clockwise, B anticlockwise, C clockwise, D anticlockwise. distractors.A: each gear turns the opposite way to the one it touches: count the steps

distractors.C: turns the wrong way and divided the wrong way round

A plane leaves Sydney at 10:40 pm and the flight takes 13 hours 25 minutes. The city it flies to is 9 hours behind Sydney.
What is the local time when the plane lands?
